#5672. Are There Any V12 Engines That Could Be Called 'Dependable?'

A V12 engine under the bonnet is a symbol of automotive decadence, telling the world that you've made it and who cares about fuel consumption. Sure, there are plenty of engines that deliver as much performance, but few that exude extravagance and luxury in quite the same way. Still, can V12s be dependable? You might assume not, given their specialized nature and low-volume production.

V12s are installed in high-end sedans and limousines, in mid-engined supercars, and in a handful of opulent SUVs and 4x4s. But they're not that numerous in the grand scheme of production vehicles.

One of the first uses of the V12 came in 1913, when, in the UK, Louis Coatalen, the chief engineer of Sunbeam Motor Car Company, stuffed a new type of aircraft engine called the Mohawk into one of the company's race cars. Subsequently, "Toodles V" was born: a machine which, after a few hiccups, went on to set eight world speed-over-distance records at Brooklands racetrack.

After Toodles and before WWII, V12s grew in popularity for their smoothness and power, with the North American auto industry providing the bulk of them, even during the Great Depression of 1929: think Packard Twin Six, the Auburn 12, the Cadillac V-12, and the Lincoln series K.

But when Lincoln ceased production of the V12 in 1948, that was that for American V12s. No car company has made one in the U.S. since, and production was mainly left to Europe. Ferrari made its legendary "Colombo" V12, Lamborghini's 1963 V12 would eventually underpin the gorgeous Miura, and even Jaguar brought a 5.3-liter V12 engine to the E-Type in 1971.

There are still a few V12s in production today that you can buy with a new-car warranty, which are likely reliable, but what about those of yesteryear? Here's a look at the most dependable.

If you're after a V12 that's about as widespread and dependable as can be, then the Mercedes M120 is the one to seek out. Mercedes had been working on the idea of a passenger car with a V12 since the 1950s (and considered putting one in its 600 Pullman limo), but it was beaten to the punch by BMW's adoption of the 5.0-liter V12 in 1987's E32 750i. Mercedes didn't get its M120 V12 to market until 1991 in the W140-series S-Class. The 600 badge was given to the W140-series S-Class, the related CL coupe, and the R129 Mercedes SL due to the engine's displacement.

The M120 was a considerably more advanced engine than BMW's V12. It featured an aluminum-alloy block, a forged crankshaft, and LH-Jetronic fuel injection, along with dual throttle bodies, mass airflow sensors, and ECUs. Producing 402 horsepower and 428 pounds-feet of torque, the M120 had enough grunt to push the heavy 600 SE and SEL models from 0 to 60 mph in around six seconds.

What makes the M120 so desirable today, though, is its dependability. There are a few known weak points, such as oil leaks around the valve covers, the front timing covers, the lower oil pan, and the front crank seal, along with worn engine mounts. But aside from these relatively minor issues, this V12 is known for its reliability and solidity. Furthermore, owners of such high-end Mercs are likely to have kept up with their maintenance.

One final seal of approval comes in the form of the M120's subsequent use in the middle of the Pagani Zonda, a supercar classic we'll always love: a 7.3-liter development of the V12 powered various iterations, culminating in a near-800-hp final edition.

Japan is a country that has not wholeheartedly embraced the V12 engine. In fact, it has made but one road-going engine of this configuration in history, although it turns out to be one of the most reliable V12s you could imagine. It's called the 1GZ-FE, a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter lump with variable valve timing, two ECUs, and enough redundancy built in that it can run on one bank of six cylinders if necessary. The engine powered the second-generation Toyota Century.

A big plus point of the 1GZ is that it's not what you'd call a stressed V12. In its original 1997 incarnation for the Century model, the Japanese "gentleman's agreement" put in place to prevent a horsepower war meant that Toyota claimed a peak power output of just 276 horsepower, with torque rated at up to 355 pounds-feet. It was never going to be one of the most powerful JDM engines ever made, even if its horsepower was higher than the domestic advertising suggested.

If that's not a big enough perk, know that like so many Toyota engines, the 1GZ-FE would accommodate a heck of a lot of tuning. In fact, the notorious Smokey Nagata – founder of Top Secret and the man who pushed a Supra to 194 mph on a British motorway in 1998 – later built another Supra with a Century's V12 in it. Only that was adorned with a pair of HKS GT2540 turbos, liberating 930 hp and a top speed of over 220 mph.

When the engine was launched, Toyota published an engineering paper stating, amongst other things, that the 1GZ-FE was more reliable than its competitors, and though the sample size is small, it has been proven to be a dependable V12, with nothing other than age-related failures of minor parts generally reported.

The original BMW V12, the M70, started an entire line of engines that went into the 7 Series as well as the 8 Series. BMW's M70 successor, the M73, was employed by Rolls-Royce starting in 1998 with the Silver Seraph. Rolls began using a V12 in its Phantom III (1936-1939), but after trying that 7.3-liter monster out for size, it eventually dedicated itself to inline-6 and V8 engines. Rolls-Royce did not use a V12 again until the 1998 Silver Seraph.

Perhaps the most famous application of a BMW V12 was the S70/2, designed by Paul Rosche, which was the incredible engine that powered the legendary McLaren F1 with 627 horsepower. Though maintenance costs are high, the engine itself is robust.

Both Ferrari and Lamborghini's V12s are highly tuned, and of course, they're installed in the sorts of cars that command huge fees on the used market. Nonetheless, the 5.5-liter engine in the Ferrari 456 GT, for example, is supposed to be fairly dependable, as long as it is subjected to regular (and expensive) maintenance.

Aston Martin has been making production V12s since the DB7 Vantage of 1999, and while these "AML" units were not just two Ford Duratec V6s welded together, there was plenty of Ford-derived DNA in the British engine courtesy of Ford's advanced powertrain division. It's generally dependable, so long as owners keep up with maintenance. Oil starvation to the crankshaft is one of the more common issues.

Finally, Jaguar had a good array of V12s in such cars as the E-Type and XJ models. While the mechanicals are reasonably durable, these engines are frequently let down by their electrics.

#5670. Slate Sells 'Screenless GPS' For Its Trucks, Which Is Just A Map

Slate, maker of the barebones $26,400 electric truck that I desperately want to see succeed despite my worries about its competition, is all about simplicity. Simple truck, simple purchase price, simple construction, simple accessories. So what happens when buyers want something more complex — something like GPS, which requires satellite connections, maps, screens, and code? Well, the company does it the old fashioned way by stamping its brand on a Rand McNally Road Atlas and selling it as "Screenless GPS."

The automaker is selling these atlases for $30, and on the website it's currently marked as sold out. The product description reads, "This is the original navigation system — no signal required. Spiral bound, large print, and ready for wherever your Slate takes you. Covers the US, Canada, and Mexico. Limited edition." This particular book is the 2027 Rand McNally EasyFinder Road Atlas, and it includes "7 curated Rand McNally road trips."

Rand McNally, for the younger readers out there, makes books of maps that it calls its road atlases. I grew up with a road atlas wedged between the driver's seat and center console of my mom's car, and I certainly remember thumbing through its pages while bored — behavior my mom encouraged, so I'd know how to read a map by the time I started driving myself. It's certainly a skill the average Slate buyer has, and maybe the folks that appreciate a simple truck will likewise appreciate a simple way to navigate it around.

Paper maps have had a bit of a renaissance as we all get ever more tired of our constantly-increasing screentime. Backcountry Discovery Routes has worked with Butler Maps for years to create paper maps of its BDR routes for those looking to go screenless on the trails, and it seems Slate is hoping to bring the same enthusiasm to road maps with its Rand McNally tie-in. I'm just hoping the promotion Slate is doing for its map, like the Instagram post above, is all tongue in cheek. If the company really means "analog pinch to zoom" is a feature, it comes off a bit I HATE WIFE AND PHOEN.

For most of us, a phone mount suction-cupped to the windshield will make a better navigation solution than a Rand McNally shoved next to the center console. For Slate's target market, buyers who actively miss simpler, older cars and want a return to that kind of design, the bent and worn pages of a worn Road Atlas may provide a bit of the nostalgia they're looking for in an all-electric truck. After all, they probably had one in their old Ranger all those years ago.

#5669. Trump Forces 7th Expensive Old Coal Power Plant To Stay Open

When a power plant gets old enough and is inefficient and expensive, it should be shut down. When it’s time to close, it’s time to close. As we’ve learned about the severe health costs and climate costs of old coal power plants, that’s even more obviously the case with them. But not for Donald Trump.

For some reason, Trump is obsessed with trying to bring the United States backward by several decades. That means, among other things, that he hates solar and wind power and he wants coal to rule again. Since coal power has become uncompetitive, he’s been using wacky logic to force old coal power plants to stay open while also paying off wind power companies to the tune of billions of dollars to not turn on power plants they’ve built. Trump’s logic with the coal plants is that we are in an energy emergency and urgently need the power — but aside from that being ridiculous, how can he then justify going and blocking wind and solar power plants from being finished and connected to the grid?

The Sierra Club updates us on this latest absurdity: “On Friday, November 13, the Trump Department of Energy issued yet another illegal ’emergency’ order, forcing the J.H. Campbell power plant to remain online. The Department issued that order despite the D.C. Circuit court ‘s decision in September rejecting the Department’s claim to ‘vast, top-down emergency power to pick its favorite generators to run at all costs.’

“This would be the power plant’s seventh order from the administration, despite no evidence that the plant has ever been needed to avoid a grid emergency or has ever prevented power outages. The extension order continues to cost families in the midwest region more than $600,000 per day to keep the old and toxic coal plant online.

“According to the Sierra Club’s Burning Money tracker, the Trump administration’s unlawful extensions have cost Americans well over half a billion dollars. Of that, over $326 million comes from J.H. Campbell based on reported utility cost recovery filings for portions of the facility’s extension orders.”

Half a billion dollars! At a time when Americans are struggling with high costs, Trump has forced expensive old coal power plants to keep running and has thus cost us half a billion dollars. And one wonders how a gigantic llue tsunami took over the country. Here’s more:

“At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing,” said Sierra Club Senior Advisor Jessi Eidbo. “Families cannot afford to pay even more for electricity, especially when what they are paying for is a dated, defunct, deadly fossil fuel plant. #5668. 1969 Chevy Camaro SS For Sale With 10,000 Miles Shown Boasts 396 V8 And Body-Up Restoration

While we're yearning for another generation of the legendary Chevrolet Camaro, our best bet is to look back at its golden era — and one of the most pristine restomods we've found on Hemmings. This Ontario orange 1969 Camaro SS, listed by a Clarkston, Michigan dealer for $58,900, shows 10,000 miles on the odometer and a body-up restoration. Its 396 big-block raises a fair question: How did that engine really stack up against its rivals back in '69?

Neither the Hemmings listing nor the dealer's YouTube walkaround gives horsepower or torque figures, but this clearly isn't a stock motor. The 396 wears an Edelbrock Performer aluminum intake, ceramic headers, a mild camshaft, and a Flame Thrower high-energy-ingition distributor, with chrome valve covers and an air cleaner on top. Behind it, a Turbo-Hydramatic 400 automatic sends power to a 10-bolt rear axle with 3.23 gears.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j-bnQtJsNGQ]

For context, Chevrolet offered three 396s in the 1969 SS, rated at 325, 350, and 375 horsepower, with torque between 410 and 415 pound-feet. The 375-horsepower L78 sat at the top, peaking at 5,600 rpm. So without a dyno sheet, there's no telling where this restomod example lands among them.

On paper, the L78 outgunned most of its competition. Its 375 horsepower beat the 345 claimed for Pontiac's Ram Air IV Firebird or the 335 rated for Mustang Mach 1's 428 Cobra Jet — one of the most powerful powertrains the Mach 1 ever came with. Even the base 325-horsepower SS 396 sat within 10 horsepower of the Cobra Jet.

Testing was less flattering. Car Life's figures (per Curbside Classic), recorded in showroom-stock trim, have a Camaro SS 396 L78 reaching 60 mph in 6.8 seconds and covering the quarter-mile in 14.77 seconds at 98.7 mph. The Mach 1 428, meanwhile, managed 5.5 seconds and 13.9 at 103.3 mph. Two other 375-horsepower rivals also ran quicker quarter-miles: the Plymouth 'Cuda 440 at 14.01 seconds, and the Boss 429 Mustang at 14.09, despite a slower 7.1-second run to 60. Traction was the usual culprit, since bias-ply tires struggled with big-block torque, so gross ratings didn't settle the pony car argument.

The Camaro's paint is Ontario orange metallic with a black hockey stripe, and there are front and rear spoilers, a cowl hood, and dual chrome mirrors. The 17-inch American Racing Torque Thrust wheels are wrapped in Dunlop 255/45ZR17 tires in back and 235/40R17s up front. The car also gets tubular upper and lower control arms, an aluminum radiator, power steering, and power front discs with slotted and drilled rotors. Inside, the black vinyl interior includes factory bucket seats, a center console, a sport steering wheel, and a Retrosound radio. So while we speculate on the return of the Camaro, consider looking to the past to get the edge off with this low-mile time capsule.

#5667. SolarEdge unveils U.S.-made optimizer for C&I solar

By Marie DeFreitas, Contributor | November 17, 2026

SolarEdge’s new Duo Power Optimizer promises to simplify commercial and industrial solar installations with 50% fewer optimizer units, independent module-level power tracking, and enhanced safety features.

The commercial and industrial (C&I) solar market is getting a new hardware option aimed at making installations simpler without sacrificing system performance. SolarEdge Technologies has unveiled its new Duo Power Optimizer, a U.S.-manufactured solution designed to deliver module-level energy harvesting and monitoring while cutting the number of power optimizers in half.

Announced November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the new product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules. Notably, each module retains its own independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT), which preserves the module-level performance benefits associated with the traditional one-to-one optimizer configurations.

For developers, EPCs and installers managing large-scale rooftop and distributed generation projects, the value here lies in fewer components to purchase, wire and install, with no trade-off in module-level optimization.

Simplifying installation without sacrificing performance

SolarEdge’s optimization tech addresses the challenge of conventional string inverter systems, which is that an underperforming module can affect the output of an entire string. But by allowing each module to operate independently, the system limits the impact of shading, degradation or performance differences between panels.

The Duo brings demonstrates that capability in a two-module configuration. By reducing the number of optimizers by 50% compared with one-to-one designs, SolarEdge is targeting an opportunity to streamline balance-of-system requirements and reduce the installation labor.

SolarEdge’s U.S.-made Duo Power Optimizer connects two solar modules while maintaining independent module-level power tracking for commercial and industrial solar installations. Credit: SolarEdge

The hardware also incorporates design changes intended to improve jobsite efficiency. Each optimizer features two input pairs: a shorter connection for the nearest module and a pre-extended connection for the adjacent module. The arrangement reduces excess wiring and eliminates the need for field-made jumpers.

The configuration also accommodates modules with different orientations, making it particularly relevant for east-west and dual-tilt racking applications.

Beyond installation efficiency, SolarEdge is emphasizing electrical safety as a central feature of the new product.

The Duo extends the company’s Sense Connect technology to its input and output connectors, monitoring connector temperatures to identify developing issues before they potentially escalate into overheating or electrical arcs.

Also, the optimizer introduces what SolarEdge describes as an industry-first approach to arc fault detection: every optimizer acts as an individual arc sensor. Rather than relying exclusively on detection at the inverter, the system distributes monitoring throughout the array, allowing potential arc faults to be identified closer to their source.

SolarEdge says the technology provides coverage across strings with up to 3,280 feet of total cable length between the inverter and optimizer. It can also help pinpoint problems to the optimizer area, potentially making troubleshooting and maintenance more efficient.

Manufactured at SolarEdge’s Florida facility, the Duo is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements, according to the company. SolarEdge says its domestic-content eligibility levels are consistent with those of its previous U.S.-manufactured power optimizers, subject to applicable tax guidance and project-specific requirements.

For SolarEdge, the Duo represents an effort to combine three priorities that are becoming more and more important in commercial solar: installation efficiency, system-level safety, and domestic manufacturing.

The technology does not fundamentally change the value proposition of module-level optimization. Instead, it looks to make that architecture more economical and easier to deploy at scale.

SolarEdge will showcase the Duo Power Optimizer at RE+ 2026.

#5666. XPENG Forecasts 45% Sales Growth in 4th Quarter

XPENG just reported 3rd quarter financial details today, while also forecasting what will happen in the 4th quarter. Everything is looking quite rosy at the moment.

As far as 3rd quarter financials go, on the back of strong sales, the company logged 24.28 billion yuan ($3.643 billion) of revenue. That’s a new quarterly record for the company. It’s 19% more than in Q3 2025 and 23% more than Q2 2026.

That said, despite strong revenue, the company still scored a net loss. It had a significant 870 million yuan ($130.5 million) net loss, in fact, which was up 128% from 380 million yuan in Q3 2025 and down 35% from 1.34 billion from Q2 2026. XPENG made a small profit in Q4 2025, and since then has again been trying to get its finances into the green again instead of in the red.

Good news going into the 4th quarter is the company expects even better. XPENG is forecasting 169,000 to 174,000 vehicle deliveries, which would mean year-over-year growth of 45% to 50%. Expected revenue is 30.4 billion yuan to 31.8 billion yuan, which would mean growth of 37% to 43%.

We’ll see. The company is still not expected to get another net profit quarter, but perhaps the quarter could surprise and XPENG could log its second quarterly profit. One thing making that unlikely, though, is that XPENG’s R&D costs were up significantly, 17.5%. Also, general and administrative expenses were up 11.4% year over year. We’ll see what the 4th quarter brings.

#5665. Mercedes Is Auctioning Off A C111 For The First Time Ever, And It'll Be Your Last Chance To Buy One For At Least 25 Years

Back in 2022, Mercedes-Benz brought a chosen group of collectors to its Museum for a secret auction, at which one of the two 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupés was sold for a record-breaking €135 million, about $143 million according to exchange rates at the time. Most people, myself including, thought there was no way Mercedes would have ever sold one of the Uhlenhauts, not to mention many of the other slightly less rare and iconic cars in its collection. Now that it had auctioned off its most valuable car, it opened up so much speculation: What could be next?

Turns out the next thing is another completely unexpected sale. On Tuesday night, at an event kicking off the week's Rétromobile New York festivities, Mercedes-Benz announced that in just a few months it will be selling one of its groundbreaking C111 prototypes. This will be the first time Mercedes has ever sold a C111, and unlike the Uhlenhaut, it will be a public auction held at RM Sotheby's Rétromobile Paris sale in February, with all proceeds going towards funding the future of the Mercedes-Benz Museum.

While I don't think the C111 will touch the Uhlenhaut's record hammer price, you really should never say never. There's no precedent for how much this car could go for, especially given that Mercedes-Benz has promised it won't sell or auction off another C111 for at least 25 years. If you want one, now might be your only chance, and the C111 in question is perhaps the best one of the bunch.

As a bit of a memory refresher, the first C111 was introduced to the public at the 1969 International Motor Show in Frankfurt, though a few were already built by then, and an updated version was shown the following year in Geneva. It was strictly an experimental vehicle, a testbed for future technology, design and powertrain ideas. Prospective customers handed Mercedes blank checks to get a C111 of their own, and Mercedes says there was "enormous public interest," but the C111 was never put into production. The company cites the 1973 oil crisis, new emissions standards and high production costs as the reasons why, but that didn't stop Mercedes from continuing to build more new versions.

Between 1969 and 1978, Mercedes built 17 different C111s across three iterations of the model: the C111-I, the C111-II, and the C111-III. The C111 was originally conceived with a rotary powertrain, first a three-rotor Wankel with later versions getting a four-rotor engine. One was built with a V8 and another has since been converted to have a V8, and the last few C111-IIIs had five-cylinder turbodiesels with which they set a bunch of records at Nardò. Three of the C111s were dismantled after testing, and one was destroyed in crash testing; the rest have remained in Mercedes' collection ever since, with only a couple of them being still functional.

As Mercedes continued building new iterations of the C111, the overall design and various details evolved, but every C111 was spectacular and clearly part of the same family. The company had never made a mid-engined sports car, not to mention anything such a wild wedge shape, so it's no surprise they were show-stoppers everywhere. Some C111s had their glass-fiber-reinforced plastic bodywork originally painted white, and the last few were metallic silver, but the cars are best known for the Weißherbst paint worn by the vast majority of them — "white autumn" in German, named after a traditional copper-tinted rosé.

The C111 being sold is a C111-II, car number 33, which Mercedes says is "only of internal significance." Production began in March 1970 with the car being completed in August, when it became the second C111-II to go into the test fleet. It was fitted with a 2.4-liter four-rotor Wankel engine that produced a massive 345 horsepower and 289 pound-feet of torque, sending the 2,734-pound car from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds and on to a top speed of 186 mph (300 km/h), making it the fastest car in the world at the time. In fact, chief test engineer Hans Liebold once hit 188 mph on the Autobahn heading towards Baden-Baden.

Mercedes says Car 33 "was used to test a fluidic component designed to ensure even emptying of the two side fuel tanks, which have a combined capacity of 30.6 gallons, to carry out temperature measurements in the rear trunk, and to conduct test drives at the Hockenheimring." It was featured on the first German issue of Playboy in 1972, and since 1975 it has been retired, part of Mercedes-Benz's collection. When the museum opened in 2006, the car has been on display in the Fascination Design area, floating on a plinth surrounding a curved staircase.

In 2024, the Mercedes-Benz Classic team in Fellbach gave Car 33 a full restoration, making it one of just a couple C111s that actually still run, and the only running car with a rotary engine. The mechanical restoration was completed without messing up the car's lovely patina, the only addition to the car being a fire extinguisher. It has the original paint and houndstooth cloth seats, and a Becker Europa radio that actualy works.

There are 24,766 kilometers on the odometer (about 15,389 miles), and Mercedes says that while Car 33 was used to test anti-lock braking systems, the ABS currently doesn't work. The car comes with its original magnesium racing wheels, sized 10x15-inch in front and 13x15-inch in the rear, but they are "not only suitable for display purposes," so Mercedes created a new set of 8x15 light alloy wheels that the car can actually be driven on. The rear trunk tub, which is designed to hold luggage, is fitted and able to be removed.

I'm particularly excited to see how much this car goes for because I've had a few very special experiences with C111s, including this specific one. Mere days before the world shut down in 2020, I was given a tour of Mercedes' secret "holy halls" warehouses in Germany, where I saw half of all the C111s all lined up together. (The photo you see below, which Mercedes graciously let me take on a film camera.)

At Monterey Car Week in 2022 I got to ride shotgun the V8-powered C111 on the Tour d'Elegance, which was incredible even when we were stuck in traffic and slightly overheating. In 2024, I got to ride up and down Big Sur in this particular car, number 33, fresh off its restoration with a fully functioning rotary engine. The V8 C111 already felt extraordinary, but the four-rotor motor's totally unique buzzy sound and character really takes it to the stratosphere. There's no other car in existence quite like it.

Apart from other C111s, of course. Yes, it's pretty nuts that Mercedes is selling one of these things, but it will still have 12 others in the collection. I'm sure now that the Classic team got this one working, it will be able to restore one of the other rotary-powered C111s in the collection. Don't think this is the last the world will see of this C111, either. Part of the buyer contract for the Uhlenhaut was that its new owner must bring the car to events and shows, and that Mercedes gets to use it for things when it wants, and I'm sure the same will be the case for this sale.

Whoever buys it really should use it, too. For all of its fantastical styling and engineering, it's a proper car. Sure, the rotary doesn't really like sitting around at low speeds, instead egging you on to keep reaching the red mark at 7,000 rpm on the tachometer, and there's no air conditioning so your only respite from in-cabin heat is to open the small vent windows (or just open the gullwing doors). It's pretty comfortable, though, and pretty easy to get in and out of. The engine isn't so loud that you can't hold a conversation with your passenger, and the interior just feels like any other Mercedes from the '70s.

The C111 be will be sold on February 3, 2027, at the Salles du Carrousel underneath the Louvre, where RM Sotheby's typically has its Rétromobile auction. RM Sotheby's says bids can be placed by phone or in person at the auction, after reigstering ahead of time of course, and if you're interested you can go to the Mercedes Classic Center website to learn about "the terms and conditions of participation, bidder registration and opportunities for pre-inspection." Given the C111's existence as a forward-thinking experiment, I think it's fitting that the money goes toward making the automaker's museum even better for future generations. Says Mercedes:

The aim of "Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0" is to bring the brand's unique heritage to life for future generations and make it accessible worldwide. To this end, Mercedes-Benz is continuously developing both the Museum in Stuttgart and its virtual offerings. A key component is the Museum's digital twin. This makes the Museum experience accessible regardless of physical location, thereby extending its reach far beyond Stuttgart. It will give people all over the world greater access to the Mercedes-Benz brand heritage. The virtual twin is being developed in collaboration with The Classic Car Trust (TCCT) and its digital platform, Roarington.

"With 'Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0' , we are consistently taking our Museum to the next level. We are continuing to write our company and brand history right up to the present day, creating new exhibition experiences and providing space for topics that are of particular interest to our visitors – from more recent classic cars to the latest innovations. With a digital twin, we are also opening up the Museum to people all over the world. Visitors can also experience the exhibits interactively here. The first results will be visible as early as 2027." -Bettina Haussmann, Director of the Mercedes-Benz Museum

So, how much could it go for? Who the hell knows. The collector car market is so absurd these days — McLaren F1s are $35-million cars now — and there's no prior sales of cars that you can really compare the C111 to. Last year the Indianapolis Motor Speedway auctioned off a Mercedes-Benz W196 R race car that become the second-most-expensive sale ever, also in parnership with the automaker and RM Sotheby's. The most expensive public sale of a Ferrari 250 GTO has been just under $52 million, while private sales have been rumored to exceed $70 million, and I think the C111 could easily clear that mark.

For its part, Mercedes says that "for at least 25 years, this will remain the only opportunity: Mercedes-Benz has contractually committed not to sell any further C111s during this period." That's definitely an incentive for people to keep raising their paddles. I'm also going to take this sale as confirmation that Mercedes is definitely working on a C111-inspired supercar in the vein of the Vision One-Eleven concept from a few years ago.

#5664. AI Writes Better Discharge Summaries Than Doctors, Study Suggests

— Physician reviewers gave AI summaries higher marks for accuracy, completeness, clarity, and tone

Artificial intelligence (AI) outperformed clinicians in drafting hospital discharge summaries, a U.K.-based retrospective study showed.

A higher proportion of large language model (LLM)-generated discharge summaries were signed off by a clinician reviewer with no or minor changes compared with clinician-authored summaries (92.2% versus 70.0%), meeting prespecified noninferiority criteria, reported Kathleen Goldsmith, MSc, senior data scientist at a partnership between Imperial College London and Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust in the U.K., and colleagues.

Moreover, clinician reviewers rated LLM-generated summaries higher on accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity compared to clinician-written summaries, they wrote in JAMA Network Open.

Finally, a smaller proportion of AI-generated discharge summaries contained inaccurate or incomplete information compared with ones written by clinicians (26.2% vs 45.1%), they reported.

"Together, these findings suggest that AI-assisted documentation could strengthen the quality of information transferred at discharge, an important component of safe and effective continuity of care," Goldsmith told MedPage Today.

While this research focused on discharge summaries, Goldsmith said it could be applied to other administrative tasks, but "patient safety and clinical value have to be central to how we adopt technology like this."

In an accompanying editorial, Melanie Molina, MD, of the University of California San Francisco, wrote that this research raises the question not of whether AI can produce acceptable drafts, but whether physicians can verify the information in real-time.

"Lengthy, complex, and fragmented clinical records create a verification paradox: the cases in which automated summarization is most valuable are often the cases in which verification is most difficult," Molina wrote, adding that emergency department care poses particular challenges.

Plus, AI tools have already evolved far beyond the model tested in this study, with newer, more sophisticated models less likely to hallucinate.

Molina argued that while this research shows that "a thoughtfully designed LLM pipeline can produce discharge summaries that clinicians prefer to routine documentation," this does not yet equate to a safer transition of care.

"The enduring clinical task will be ensuring that what it writes is true, complete, and actionable," she wrote.

Goldsmith and team sought to evaluate how AI tools could "free up clinician time for patient-facing care while maintaining clinical safety and accuracy" and to develop a framework for evaluating the use of LLMs in clinical settings.

This retrospective noninferiority study used Imperial Clinical Analytics, Research and Evaluation (iCARE) research data from a network of 5 hospitals in London from Sept. 1, 2022, to Sept. 30, 2023.

Discharge summaries written by clinicians and by GPT-4o mini were blindly reviewed by 12 resident physicians from the Imperial College Healthcare Trust. The primary outcome was clinician sign-off on the discharge summary with little to no edits. Goldsmith noted this endpoint reflects how the technology would be used in real-world settings.

"Having clinician input in both the co-design, use, and evaluation of healthcare AI technologies is crucial to ensure these systems are trusted, and truly deliver the benefits to clinical work," Goldsmith said.

Ultimately, there were 1,294 discharge summaries included, of which 649 were clinician-authored and 645 were LLM-generated.

Patients' median age was 46 and 56.6% were female. The median length of stay was 3 days. On average, each case required the review of 30 clinical documents, or about 4,000 words.

The researchers noted some limitations, including that de-identification may have removed clinically relevant information, that only one LLM was evaluated, and the retrospective study design; prospective assessments at the point of care are still needed.

#5663. BMW In South Carolina: A Free Trade Success Story

I recently attended BMW’s “Beyond The Machine” event in South Carolina. The largest facility of the German company globally is Plant Spartanburg in Greer, South Carolina. As part of the event, I saw the opening of BMW’s new battery plant in nearby Woodruff. We stayed in the nearby city of Greenville, which was transformed by BMW and the businesses that followed.

Beyond the vehicles and manufacturing, which I plan to cover in more detail in future articles, one of the most striking aspects was the human impact. From the “Woodruffian” Mayor fighting back tears at the opening of the battery plant to the plant employees to the people I met exploring the town, they clearly appreciate what BMW has done for the community. Throughout the presentations and discussions, there was support for free trade along with the local benefits. People in the area pride themselves in their resilience. They have reason to be proud. And they were optimistic about the growth of the increasingly clean manufacturing and electrified products from this global company.

The area around Greenville, South Carolina the rose to prominence in the 1870s on the textile industry. Cotton from throughout the South that had previously been shipped to other areas for processing was processed in Greenville and Spartanburg counties. However, as global competition increased in the 20th century, the mills became less competitive. The last textile mill closed in Greenville in 1977, although a few textile operations continued in the region into the 1980’s. As that industry left, the local economy declined. If the story ended there, many might use it as an argument against free trade.

When BMW came to South Carolina in 1992, they saw a lot of potential. Michelin had already started making tires there in 1978. Local leaders were enthusiastic to work with BMW. The people were also enthusiastic to receive training for the new jobs. The deep-water port of Charleston on the other side of the state facilitated shipping, while nearby rail links connected to much of the US.

Since 1992, BMW has invested over $15.8 Billion. The new Woodruff battery plant is their most recent major investment. In the process, an area that could have been considered a casualty of global trade became one of its greatest beneficiaries.

The first model, an E36 3 series, rolled off the line in 1994. BMW also produced the Z3 in the plant, including the first “German” car driven by James Bond on camera. However, the big breakthrough came with the introduction of the X5 in 1999. At the time, relatively few SUVs were being sold in Europe. BMW Spartanburg as the center of SUV production was intending to largely for the US. However, global markets shifted.

Now, Spartanburg is the “Home of X.” It currently produces the X3, X5, X6, X7 and XM, including electrified versions. It is the sole manufacturing plant for a number of those SUV models globally. A little over half of their production is exported, which also makes it consistently the top US overseas automotive exporter. Export volume topped $9 Billion in 2025 over roughly 200,000 X vehicles.

BMW designed those vehicles to be able to use ICE, PHEV and BEV powertrains. While some may want them to make just pure BEV, the approach gives BMW the ability to shift rapidly with the market. The different models also give the plant a level of market resilience. However, to fuel that resilience they need a very flexible supply chain that can respond quickly. Suppliers being close to the plant creates greater resilience.

BMW is designing its vehicles to be globally competitive. While 400+ miles of EPA range and charging speeds approaching 500 kW may be at the top of the US market, they are also competitive in global markets. While BMW developed the cells and packs, they use multiple suppliers to manufacture the cylindrical cells to their specifications. Packs at the plant currently use AESC cells, but they will shift to LG in the future and use other suppliers in other markets.

BMW also worked with the state of South Carolina to develop people. Nearby Clemson University provides a source of engineering talent, and BMW partners with the university on the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research, where both students and BMW benefit from the development of new innovations. They are also developing potential future suppliers with the BMW Venture funds. One such company will be supplying flax-based composites to future M models.

A heavy emphasis is placed on technical training at the factory. In addition, they collaborated with community colleges to provide technical training. But the development programs start much earlier, with a heavy emphasis in middle school and sponsoring the First Robotics Competition for elementary school students.

BMW also worked with the South Carolina Department of Transportation to build infrastructure to support the plant and its suppliers. Moving forward, that infrastructure will increasingly include electrification and EV charging. BMW also worked with the SC Ports Authority to develop an “inland port,” which is essentially a direct rail link to the Port of Charleston. By moving freight by rail, emissions are greatly reduced. In addition, a lot of emphasis is going into transferring freight quickly, as every minute a truck sits idling is also wasted emissions.

While BMW employs 11,000 workers, over four times as many jobs are supported by the plant, according to a Clemson economist. That multiplier is much higher than most companies due to how BMW operates. Part of the impact on the local economy beyond employee count comes from the strategy behind the manufacturing. Overall, more than 70% of the value of the vehicles comes from outside suppliers.

Plant Spartanburg receives 3.3 million parts per day delivered by 1200 truckloads and 50 sea containers, 6 days per week. All those parts then go into over 1500 vehicles produced per day. The plant is laid out a bit different than some other manufacturing plants to facilitate the supply chain. Multiple fingers go up off the main line, along which parts are delivered to be assembled nearby. There isn’t much in the way of warehousing. Trucks come to the plant each day and the parts can end up on vehicles driving off the line the same day.

In the initial stages of manufacturing, more of the supply base came from overseas. However, as the plant established itself, more suppliers localized. That growing supply chain then attracted additional companies to the region, like Mercedes, Volvo and Scout. Those companies then create greater scale for the suppliers, who can reduce costs and expand operations.

Overall, for heavy, bulky components, localization will tend to  happen naturally. For a company that relies on suppliers to consistently and almost constantly deliver parts, that localization tends to increase. The more localized the supply chain, the more capable it becomes to respond to market dynamics. Once scale is attained for heavy, bulky components like batteries, that production will naturally become more localized.

BMW has a growing supply chain footprint across the Americas and especially across the Southeastern US. There will be over 850 Tier 1 supplier locations in the Americas by 2027, with multiple times as many Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers providing materials, parts and components. BMW focuses on value creation, competitiveness and collaboration in their supply chain. In addition, while they are bringing economic benefit, they are also focused on decarbonization.

Of course, all this economic activity has brought “green” in terms of money to the local communities. As I was stranded in Greenville due to flight interruptions, I had time to walk around the town and speak to some of the locals. Streets that were once desolate and unsafe are now vibrant with shops and restaurants. An area that people once wanted to leave is now growing rapidly and attracting people from around the world. I started conversations  with several friendly people in town about trade. I heard stories of transformation from past struggles to current successes.

Even though it was clear that they were benefitting from the economic impact, I was still surprised how strongly and openly they supported free trade and realized the benefits. A local guide pointed out major buildings and businesses that were new. Downtown is now pleasant and walkable. Part of that is due to the restoration of a river that runs through the city, surrounded by shops and artwork, where I saw some locals fishing in the clear water. This gets to the other kind of “green.”

While there are a lot of trucks transporting materials and components, shortened travel distances and efforts to streamline intermodal transfers reduce emissions. The proximity enables packaging to typically be sent back to the supplier to be reused. BMW is also putting a lot of effort into reduced CO2 emissions steel produced locally, which I plan to follow up on. Over half the steel in their vehicles is reduced CO2. Solar panels and landfill gas provide power for their facilities.

As the company relies heavily on its supply chain, the supply chain is a major focus of its decarbonization strategy. While EVs reduce emissions overall, the proportion of emissions from the manufacturing phase tends to be higher than for ICE vehicles, adding emphasis to decarbonization of manufacturing. At the same time, they strive to create regional strength, resilience and value creation while reducing emissions. Close collaboration is the key to meeting these goals. BMW plans to have net zero CO2 emissions throughout their supply chain by 2050 at the latest.

The new Woodruff plant will produce their sixth-generation battery. BMW develops the batteries first and then outsources the cell manufacturing, but they will now be manufacturing the packs locally. Initially, this will be for the iX5, to be delivered domestically and to global markets. However, additional EV models may benefit in the future.

Overall, politicians in the 1970’s could have tried to block global competition to protect the textile mills. That might have extended the life of those plants for a few years. However, in the process, those plants would become less globally competitive and less globally relevant. Protectionism would have only extended a slow, painful decline.

However, by keeping the market open and staying open to new business opportunities, Greenville, Greer, Spartanburg and Woodruff created the circumstances for their current success. People were open to new companies from other countries. They were open to industries that were new to the area. And they were open to investing in retraining to better take advantage of the new opportunities.

In the initial site selection, South Carolina could have imposed strict regulations and tried to force localization before the factory was built, production was ramped up and scale was attained to support that localization. If that happened, the plant would have undoubtedly been built elsewhere, and the economic benefits would have gone to someone else. By taking a more collaborative approach, rather than being confrontational, both BMW and local suppliers benefitted greatly. Building on that approach, more companies came to the region, building scale and amplifying the benefits.

BMW is not being hypocritical in their support of free trade. They are not promoting free trade just when it benefits them and then putting up barriers for other competitors. They are not shying away from global competition. They are seeking to make globally competitive vehicles for global markets. While global competition is fierce, by facing that competition, rather than hiding from it, their products become more competitive.

In the process, one of the brightest spots in US automotive trade globally, as well as one of the leaders in electrified product and supply chain decarbonization, comes from a German company.

Change and globalization can be scary things. Especially in the short term. The transition to EVs can also be scary, especially for those tied to the past. However, hiding behind political and trade walls rarely works out in the long run. A willingness to be open and collaborative with people who might come from within different lines on a map or sound different than you can have long term benefits. And the courage to engage with the technology transition and compete globally can put you ahead of many established competitors. That cannot only transform how we power our vehicles, but also transform the lives of people in communities for generations to come. As Woodruff Mayor Kenneth Gist put it at the battery plant opening:

BMW and the City of Woodruff wanted the same thing. Success in business, success in our community, and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world…

…When I think about this plant, I think about our children, our grandchildren. Educational partnership that will open the doors for them, the career that will be waiting for them, and a Woodruff they would be proud to call home for decades to come. BMW, you have been a true partner to me personally, to every person in this community.

Larry lives in Queens, NY, with his wife and cats. While he has spent much of his professional career leading global marketing efforts, his passions focus on clean technology and the automotive industry. He believes in Green Free Trade and the potential for the application of engineering talent to create solutions to the world’s most challenging problems.

#5662. 7 Engine Swaps Where The Exhaust Note Will Make You Do A Double Take

A lot of really cool cars come straight out of the factory, but for those who want something truly unique, or just love a bizarre challenge, an obscure engine swap is often the best direction in which to head. Now, here at Jalopnik we've covered no end of awesome conversions in the past, including documenting your dream engine swaps, but this list focuses on something a little more specific.

The list is full of engine swaps which we love, purely because they wind up giving the base car an exhaust note that nobody would ever expect. Included among the 7 is a VR6-swapped Porsche 911 with more than 1,000 horsepower, and a Korean city car with a GM-sourced V6 wedged under the smallest hood imaginable. And to prove our point, each feature engine swap is accompanied with a video to demonstrate just how absurd these swaps are.

Before you race to the comments to point out all the cool swaps we have missed, it's also worth mentioning that we paid particularly close attention to projects which, from the outside at least, looked largely stock. Or, if not stock, at least they weren't giving the secret away. So, no superchargers protruding through hoods here, or turbos masquerading as headlights. In no particular order, these are 7 of the most double-take-worthy engine swaps we found, kicking things off with a Ferrari-powered DeLorean that sure would have given Doc Brown a far easier time in cracking that 88 mph threshold in the "Back To The Future" films.

Almost everything about the factory-original DeLorean is awe-inspiring. The brushed stainless steel bodywork, the rakish lines, and, of course, the silver-screen connection that immortalized the model forever as Doc Brown's time machine. However, its 130-hp 2.8-liter V6 has always been a source of disappointment in the eyes of many. Put simply, the DeLorean always deserved better.

A firm by the name of FuelTech took it upon themselves to address this concern. This particular vehicle did not have an engine when they found it, but it would have been powered by a PRV (Peugeot-Renault-Volvo) engine.  Instead of settling for the original engine, they put in a far more exotic 4.3-liter V8. The mill itself was sourced from a Ferrari California, and delivers 453 horsepower, alongside 358 pound-feet of torque. The soundtrack that now echoes from the DeLorean's rear-end is nothing like what bystanders might expect.

Helping to distribute that power is a six-speed Tiptronic transmission, pinched from a Porsche 911. A KW kit addressed any and all suspension-related concerns, while a larger brake kit was also understandably called upon. The DeLorean isn't a car which usually sees such in-depth modification, with most owners choosing to keep them entirely stock, or to turn them into time machine replicas. However, this particular example was purchased by FuelTech in a sorry state, with no engine and needing much work, so it's perhaps not the purist's nightmare many might first assume.

One of the wildest Cummins swaps out there is this 4BT-swapped Toyota Prius. The Toyota would have started life with a 1.5-liter inline-four hybrid system, but that — along with the entire interior and a whole heap of metalwork — has been entirely stripped out. In its place, owner Ben Schulz dropped in a turbocharged 3.9-liter inline-four diesel Cummins engine, which dynoed at 360 hhp and 550 lb-ft of torque.

Schulz says a TDI engine and front-wheel drive was at least lightly considered at one point, but instead, the Cummins and rear-wheel drive swap idea was too good to ignore. Hearing a high-capacity turbo diesel 4-cylinder thundering down the road, which is traditionally more at home in construction vehicles, but then seeing a Prius emerging through a thick cloud of black smoke must be one of the most double-take-worthy engine swaps of all time — it's a wild swap, that's for sure.

Remarkably, the car still looks fairly standard from the outside; even the standard rear wheels were widened rather than replaced, in order to retain that factory look. Future plans include refitting as much of the original interior as possible, which should further boost the sleeper appeal of this coal-rolling Toyota.

The Chevrolet Corvette hasn't always sported a V8 engine. In fact, the first Corvettes arrived with the Blue Flame inline-six engine under their hoods, but for certain, there has never been a factory four-cylinder Corvette. However, some engineers from Unruly Motorsports decided to build exactly that, swapping a C6 Corvette's 6.0-liter LS2 out for a turbocharged four-cylinder Honda K24.

In its stock guise, the C6 Corvette produces a healthy 400 hp, but the minds behind this K24 build had their sights set an awful lot higher. Before dropping this particular K24 into the Corvette, it managed to make an impressive 828 horsepower on 20 pounds of boost. It boasts forged internals, a closed deck, and a 67mm turbocharger with ceramic ball bearings, and interestingly enough, it's hooked up to a built 2-speed Powerglide transmission. Once setup in the C6, Unruly Motorsports managed to see a peak of 917 hp on the dyno, alongside 563 lb-ft of torque.

This swap wasn't carried out just to annoy the purists, although no doubt it probably has upset a few of them. Instead, it was built to perform, and with it churning out quarter-mile passes in the very low 11-second range, it certainly does exactly that. All while turning more heads than most silver drop-top C6 Corvettes, thanks mostly to that most curious and un-GM-like four-pot soundtrack.

People have been swapping all sorts of engines into Miatas for a while now. We've seen 800-horsepower and 10,000 rpm K24-powered Miatas, and even motorcycle engine-swapped Miatas, and while those will both sound distinctly different from standard models, it's this Volvo-motivated Miata which has our interests piqued today.

Apart from a few curious graphics, this first-generation Miata looks pretty stock. It's passable for just another cheap project car, the type which are spotted fairly commonly. However, beneath the factory hood lies a B2544T engine, which belongs to the T5 family. In short, 2.4 liters, 5 cylinders, one turbocharger, a goal of between 300 and 400 horsepower, and a Miata.

Plans were originally made for a T6 engine to slot under the hood, but the T5 would fit into the available space easier. For our purposes, it suits too, as while a boosted inline-six does sound cool, the T5 boasts a particularly distinctive sound.

The engine is hooked up to a manual 6-speed transmission plucked from a BMW 1 Series, which the owners notes was chosen due to its ability to handle an awful lot of torque. The real joy of a swap like this is that it demonstrates how creativity trumps funds. Mating a cheap Miata to a junkyard Volvo motor and coupling that with an old BMW transmission is just as cool as any other swap on this list.

We've looked at this 6.2-liter LS3-powered Tesla in the past, but it certainly deserves a spot on this list too. Popular automotive YouTuber Rich Rebuilds took what was a flood-damaged Tesla Model S and mated its body with the LS3 out of a Chevrolet Camaro, while at the same time making every effort to keep it looking relatively stock from the outside. A vinyl wrap was chosen for the finished product, though, in a rather unflattering brownish color, until you realize it plays on the car's "ICE-T" nickname, which cleverly combines ICE (internal combustion engine) with T, for Tesla.

That's why, when the key is turned and that thunderous V8 soundtrack booms out of the Tesla's side-exit exhaust pipe, it's absolutely one of those engine swaps that will give bystanders cause to stop what they are doing and give this former-EV a double take.

The team dropped the LS3 into the Tesla's frunk and mated it with a sequential 6-speed manual transmission, which itself was routed through a custom-made transmission tunnel. It wound up making around 440 horsepower, and bizarrely garnered the YouTuber a lot of hate online. Remember, this was a flood-damaged car; he essentially saved it from the junkyard. After the build's completion, the V8 Tesla was passed around various YouTubers before ending up back with Rich some 5 years later. The car returned to him with numerous updates, most notably a Magnuson supercharger, in addition to a heap of issues, so it will be interesting to see how the V8-swapped Tesla's life continues from this point forward.

The Porsche 911 996 Turbo is already a powerful car, producing 415 hp and 413 lb-ft of torque as standard from its Mezger 3.6-liter flat-six engine. That engine is also really quite susceptible to tuning, with kits available from Speed Density Motorsports that can send that standard output soaring close to and even north of 1,000 horsepower.

However, Speed Density Motorsports found a way of delivering up to 1,500 horsepower from the 996 Turbo platform, but its method of securing such a figure is a little unconventional. For this, the flat-six was removed entirely, and a 3.2-liter VR6 engine – the same engine which has been doing the rounds in Volkswagen cars for over 30 years now — was dropped back into the space instead, albeit now with a wild state of tune. The engine, 3.3 liters, with billet aluminum and forged internals was installed, and a Precision 8565 ball-bearing turbocharger was fitted. Everything is new and high-end; this is a 1,500-horsepower VR6 running on methanol fuel, after all.

Footage of the outfit's Stage 4-equipped shop car, with Stage 4 being detailed as a 3.2-liter VR6-swapped single turbo build capable of cracking 1,300 horsepower on E85, shows off the unusual and aggressive exhaust note thrown out the back of this once flat-six-motivated 996. This particular generation of 911 has been the subject of other curious engine swaps in the past, but the iconic warble of a VR6 has to be the best candidate yet from a soundtrack perspective.

There aren't that many reasons to celebrate the achievements of Daewoo, certainly not from an enthusiastic perspective. The Matiz was a diminutive little four-door hatchback produced by the Korean firm from the late '90s onward, until GM purchased the automaker and production carried on as the Chevrolet Matiz. Eventually, the Spark would replace the nameplate.

As standard, a 52-horsepower 0.8-liter inline-three powered the little Matiz. It was never a performer, instead prioritizing cheapness, as most Daewoo cars did. However, one man — bored of engine-swapping Vauxhalls — decided to make a humble one-owner Matiz the subject of a seriously cool engine swap. The brief was simply to place the biggest engine possible into the smallest car available.

The engine in question was a naturally aspirated 3.2-liter V6 from a Vauxhall Vectra, which kicks out 208 horsepower and 221 lb-ft of torque, in addition to a sensationally unusual engine note for this dinky little city-dweller. Nothing to shout about, but considering a standard Matiz weighs only 1,711 pounds, the power-to-weight ratio is really quite impressive. It was understandably a tight fit under the Matiz' tiny hood, but with custom engine mounts and a modified intake manifold, the builder squeezed it in while still retaining the factory airbox.

Ample stopping power comes from a custom big brake kit on the front consisting of Focus RS rotors and Lancer Evolution VI calipers, which sit behind 18-inch Porsche alloys. A lightened flywheel and limited-slip differential make the most of the V6's power, and — aside from a Vauxhall gear-shifter — the interior has been kept entirely stock.

#5661. Mission Solar Energy puts supply chain transparency in the spotlight at RE+ 2026

By Marie DeFreitas, Contributor | November 18, 2026

With new high-efficiency residential and commercial modules and an integrated supply chain spanning polysilicon to power conversion, Mission Solar Energy is making a case for U.S. manufacturing, domestic content and FEOC-compliant sourcing.

As the solar industry continues to navigate shifting trade policies, domestic content incentives, and supply chain scrutiny, Mission Solar Energy is bringing a message of manufacturing strength and transparency to RE+ 2026. The San Antonio-based manufacturer showcased its latest commercial and residential modules while highlighting the advantages of its relationship with fellow OCI Holdings subsidiaries OCI TerraSus and OCI Power.

The announcement puts the spotlight on a growing priority for solar developers, installers and distributors: knowing exactly where components originate and having the documentation to prove it.

The three companies collectively cover significant portions of the solar value chain. OCI TerraSus produces high-purity, solar-grade polysilicon in Sarawak, Malaysia; Mission Solar designs, engineers, and assembles modules in San Antonio, Texas; and OCI Power manufactures inverters and power conversion systems in South Korea.

According to Mission Solar, all three companies are compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements and are not classified as prohibited foreign entities. The integrated structure offers customers access to a traceable supply chain backed by OCI Holdings, a global clean energy group headquartered in Seoul.

For an industry that’s becoming more and more focused on sourcing eligibility and domestic manufacturing credentials, that positioning could prove commercially important.

On the product front, Mission Solar is highlighting two modules aimed at different market segments.

For commercial and industrial (C&I) applications, the company is featuring its 595W N-Type Bifacial 144HC module. The dual-glass design captures sunlight from both sides, potentially increasing energy production without requiring additional project footprint. Designed and assembled in the United States, the module carries 11.5% domestic content, meets FEOC requirements and supports front-side loads of up to 5,400 Pa.

Residential installers will get a look at the 440W N-Type 108HC rooftop module, which Mission Solar says will be the first of its kind on the market with 12% domestic content. Building on an existing 6% domestic-content version, the module combines N-type cell technology and a multi-busbar design to deliver efficiency of up to 23%. It is also approved on residential financing platforms including LightReach and GoodLeap.

Looking further ahead, Mission Solar plans to preview two next-generation G12R modules, with commercial launches anticipated in late 2027. The company will also display a lower-domestic-content U.S.-produced C&I module option expected in 2027.

Although module performance is still critical to the industry, supply chain credibility is increasingly part of the overall purchasing decision.

As developers evaluate project economics, tax credit eligibility and sourcing risk, manufacturers that can offer transparent documentation alongside competitive technology may have an advantage.

#5660. Waymo's Latest Play To Win Over Humans To Driverless Taxis Is Women's Safety

Waymo has been burning piles of money as a Google spin-off company for a decade now with no end in sight. Technical challenges aside, what really makes or breaks a new technology is the behavior of the people using it. The company's latest reach-out to the average American arrived in ad-form last week, and it bets on women and their constantly compromised safety.

"Built for women. Designed for peace of mind," is a one-minute video following women doing all of the things we are taught to do when simply trying to move through the world — looking over the shoulder constantly, engaging in fake, one-sided conversations over the phone, getting out keys, etc. Layered in is a voiceover montage of women's voices saying all-too-common phrases uttered when a friend leaves the pack. Things like "maybe keep your keys out before you leave the bar," and "have someone walk you out to your car." The ad ends with a woman (separately) getting into a car. She shuts the the door and gives a big exhale. The Waymo is her safe space.

A Waymo robotaxi could possibly prove safer for any rider, regardless of gender, considering how faulty human drivers can be. Meanwhile, Uber's handling of its sexual assault cases would give any reasonable woman pause. Lyft and Uber even offer women-only drivers to customers because of women's understandable hesitance to get into a car with a man they don't know. So, why not expand that logic by removing the driver entirely. Waymo further backed its advantages for women's safety in its a blog saying that the company's data showed over half of female riders said that "Waymo improves their sense of personal safety. Having a space where riders are in control of their environment makes a real difference."

As a woman who has said or heard (or practiced) much of the advice in Waymo's video, I'll admit there is some comfort in not having to worry about being alone in a car with a driver. Advertising on the bet that other women will too makes me feel a cynical little queasiness in my gut, however. It's a drop in the bucket for what women have to worry about when they leave their homes. For instance, in Waymo's own video, a women walked from venue to robotaxi for some distance alone on a dark street. Should something happen in that time, a human driver might be able to spot it and intervene. A woman already has to shoulder the responsibility of her attacker's actions against her, will that scrutiny now extend to her choice in transportation?

I wanted to know more about what Waymo offers for riders in terms of safety not only in the car, but outside of it. Waymo, in response, wrote that the company takes "any situation involving threats, harassment or violence toward a rider extremely seriously."  It does, however, "... recognize that personal safety encompasses more than avoiding traffic collisions. It also involves how people experience transportation, the support available to them and their ability to make informed choices throughout a trip."

That being said, I asked Waymo how it can help riders in a variety of safety situations whether outside and inside the vehicle, taking into consideration that it's not just women who are concerned, parents might send their kids in Waymos, among many other individuals.

For instance, if a customer were attacked outside of a vehicle, there's not a ton a Waymo car can do. The rider can reach emergency services like 9-1-1 through the app or from their phones and, in some instances, Waymo says the vehicle may remain stationary until help arrives and communicate with people outside of the vehicle via its external speakers.

If a vehicle were to make a stop due to a technical issue someplace, the doors remain locked and it's recommended the rider stay in the vehicle until the issue is addressed or Waymo's Roadside Assistance arrives (if the situation requires it). In some cases a Waymo driver will arrive and get behind the wheel to help the vehicle autonomously navigate to the rider's destination.

In most any case, if something happens, riders are directed to call for assistance in the app, on their own by phone, or through the in-car screen. It's not a perfect system, as no one can control every element in every environment. The company earnestly takes it seriously though, and says it is always open to hearing more feedback.

What Waymo can't do unfortunately is fix behaviors that still remain rampant in American society in the 21st century, but hey, at least it can use the fears of those behaviors to advertise.

#5659. The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding new ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.

They recently reached out about a new stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station. It packs in a meaningful 2.5 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage capacity by itself, but the real magic is that it was built to be modular and can be linked up with additional storage modules to be stacked underneath, connecting directly to the main unit.

Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.

This modular format is a game changer because it means you don’t need an installer to bolt 300 pounds of batteries to the wall of your house. Instead, you can order them in manageable formats and add more as you need them. Among other things, this capability allows the owner to assemble and disassemble the battery pack that meets their needs when they need it.

If you’re heading out to camp for a week in your RV, you can grab an Apex 200 and one of BLUETTI’s B300K expansion batteries and bring 5.5 kWh of capacity with you on the road. When you get home from the trip, you can put them back into the garage and add that back into the battery capacity for your home.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 serves as a head unit or master controller for the battery stack, while the other battery modules are effectively servants to it. For example, when you’re setting the unit up to charge from a wall outlet or from a set of BLUETTI’s solar panels, which can wire directly into the Apex 200 with MC4 connectors, you simply plug one set of connectors or one AC charging cable into the Apex 200 and it automatically balances the energy storage across however many additional battery packs are plugged into the unit.

That really simplifies the charging structure and allows you to use the battery exactly how you want to. If you want to just head to the park with two solar panels that are portable, you can do that and have a much more manageable power system, effectively bringing a mini-grid with you on the go.

We tested the BLUETTI Apex 200 out on a wall charger and, much like most of the other portable power stations on the market, it effectively maxes out the capacity you can actually draw from a wall outlet, which is around 1,600 watts continuous. Even with the best charging cables, you’re going to notice some heat building up in the cable, and BLUETTI has made some concessions for this. The Apex 200 has a switch that allows you to select from different charging modes:

When it comes to solar, the BLUETTI Apex 200 can plug in to solar arrays through either an XT60 connector or the MC4 connectors that wire directly into the unit on the side. Between the MC4 connectors and the XT60 solar input, the unit can pull down 3,000 watts of solar, though you will need to make sure the voltage on your panels lines up with what each of the ports on the unit can handle. When we initially wired our two Bluetti 100-watt solar panels into the unit, we had them wired in parallel, which resulted in just 40 volts being pushed into the unit.

Stacking them in series gave us 80 volts, which pushed it over the minimum 60 volts for the MC4 connectors and allowed the BLUETTI Apex 200 to start charging from the panels. Pushing 2,000 watts maximum of solar power into a 5.5 kWh battery stack is going to take some time to get it charged up, but it’s easy to manage scaling the input power system up to an impressive 2,000 watts to really deliver some meaningful power.

The flexibility is pretty impressive, because it means you can dial the system in to exactly what you need, whether that’s bolting an array to the top of your RV or installing solar panels on the side of your house and then wiring them in a way that’s the most convenient for you.

BLUETTI also makes a larger B500K battery, so you can really pick and choose exactly the right level of storage that you need for your house and the right size battery packs that you want to be able to move around.

The MC4 connectors for solar panels are a little bit troublesome on the BLUETTI Apex 200 because they require a special tool to release the locks that connect the male and female ends of MC4 connectors together. That means if you have your solar panels wired up and plugged into the unit, you’ll need an MC4 connector release tool to disconnect the solar panels from the Apex 200 before you move on. Alternately, you can wire the solar panels up through an XT60 connector, which is a simple plug-and-play adapter for lower voltage solar setups.

When it came time to use the stored power from the BLUETTI Apex 200 and the B300K battery pack, we had to pick up some more high-draw appliances to really put them the the test. We bought a 1,500-watt electric fireplace and 1,500-watt portable heater for a total draw of around 3,000 watts by. We also grabbed an an Instant Pot from the kitchen to pull a bit more juice from the battery stack.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 handled both of the heaters running full blast without a problem. It shared a continuous power output capacity of 3,200 watts. This gets bumped to 3,600 watts when you attach a B300K extension battery. Beyond that, you can even pull a little bit more power, pulling peak usage up to 4,800 watts for a few seconds, because of its peak power handling capacity.

Keeping the larger heater unit attached, we added an Instapot to the the mix, and again the unit had no issues no matter what power levels we used. It’s a solid stack with impressive stats that actually deliver when you need them to the most.

BLUETTI has really built an impressive system here with the Apex 200 and its different expansion battery options. A single BLUETTI Apex 200 can be expanded up to 33.3 kWh, and they can even go bigger than that if you need something with more storage.

BLUETTI allows you to link three Apex 200 battery stacks together through their Hub 1 accessory for a total of just under 100 kWh of storage capacity. That can be accomplished by stacking three Apex 200s with a bunch of BLUETTI’s 5kWh B500Ks and then linking them all together through the Hub 1.

It’s a massive system that shows BLUETTI isn’t just building products for a quick sale, but building a much more comprehensive, flexible storage system that you can build at home into the right configuration for your needs with components that act more like LEGO building blocks.

The ability to wire in solar via XT60 connectors and MC4 connectors is exciting, giving homeowners even more options to produce power from the sun for them to run their lives on. The BLUETTI Apex 200 retails for $1,399 USD.

For more information about the BLUETTI Apex 200, the B300K, B500K expansion packs, or their solar panels, head over to their official website.
