#5557. Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings

Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hone Health, a physician-led virtual longevity care platform, has raised $228 million.

The investment is structured as a combination of equity and growth financing. The $28 million series A extension was led by MarcyPen Capital Partners, with participation from Pentland Ventures, Kinship Ventures, Hanwha, Gannet Capital, humbition and Comma Capital. Other angel investors also participated, including the Jonas brothers. The $200 million in growth financing came from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Hone will use the investment to support a number of expansions. It plans to launch more programming for metabolic health, PMOS, inflammation and immunity, and to launch a physician-supervised peptide program. It will add more diagnostics, including coronary CT angiography and gut microbiome analysis.

Hone also plans to continue building out its AI operating system that brings data together to help personalize care. And it plans to build out clinical trial infrastructure to support pharma partners.

“Longevity is thought of as this super exotic thing. […] I actually think longevity is now becoming primary care,” Saad Alam, co-founder and CEO of Hone, told Fierce Healthcare.

It costs $65 to test for 70 biomarkers with Hone, followed by a clinician consult with the option to add more diagnostics. Labs, health history, symptoms and medications are run through its AI, which then gives providers treatment recommendations. Hone can keep adding additional diagnostics and medications, per Alam, “and the AI gets smarter as we get more patients into that system.”

Additionally, Hone is publicly announcing Hone Black, a new concierge longevity membership that has operated in stealth for a select group of patients for the past year. It combines diagnostics on over 1,600 health markers with ongoing medical care from physicians. Offerings include prescriptions, supplements, peptides and lifestyle guidance, plus exosome and stem cell therapies.

Alam founded the company after experiencing a shift in his health at 35 years old, including mental health issues, depression and weight gain. His doctor was initially of little help. It took Alam a year to find out he had low testosterone, and after treatment, he finally felt back on track. That experience, along with his father dying from kidney disease and his mother going through early menopause, opened his eyes to the longevity space.

“This whole concept of longevity is going to be one of the single greatest problems I can dedicate my life to solving,” Alam realized at the time. He experimented with everything, from peptides to cold plunges to meditation.

Hone is a subsidiary of Time Therapeutics, which aims to support production of drugs that help people live longer. Alam, who started his career doing market research at Eli Lilly, knew clinical trials are expensive and inaccessible. He wanted to create a company that could help commercialize drugs. The first step to that is Hone, or a DTC virtual care company that can capture longitudinal data on patients. The next phase will be publishing research. Finally, Hone will look to partner with pharma to get drugs to market faster.

The company has been providing care for five years, treating about 200,000 patients to date. It requires patients to have a physician and get bloodwork every 90 days in order to get medication refills. Members can contact their clinician between sessions as needed.

“We make sure, for the most part, that you are doing bloodwork and talking to a physician, a real conversation with a physician, in order to get prescribed medication,” Alam said.

It isn’t about overprescribing medications. It’s about finding the most personalized protocol for each patient. “The companies that have—no pun intended—longevity are the ones that are going to figure out how to reduce the number of medications somebody might need,” Alam said.

Hone began with hormone therapy, then moved into longevity care with biomarker analysis and women’s health. Two months ago, Hone’s offerings for women surpassed offerings for men in terms of net new members. It soon plans to run clinical trials on poly-chronic patients as well to help determine the right drug at the right time. Hone crossed $100 million in revenue in 2025, per Alam, and is on track to double this year.

“When I started goop, wellness was a niche conversation,” Gwyneth Paltrow, founder and CEO of goop and co-founder of Kinship Ventures, said in a press release. “Today, it’s one of the biggest categories in the world, and the next step is bringing real health and wellness to the masses, not just the few. Saad has built Hone to do exactly that, with serious science and at real scale. That’s why Kinship invested, and we could not be more excited about what’s ahead.”

Hone will soon offer 14 longevity care categories, which Alam argues is akin to primary care. He estimates that Hone only refers to in-person care about 10% of the time, usually for higher-acuity conditions. Some Hone patients are already healthy; most are sick and willing to pay out of pocket because the current system has been inadequate in solving their health needs, per Alam.

“This is just the beginning of not only a way but a complete change in the way that medicine is practiced,” Alam said. “A lot of other companies are what I’ll call pill mills, and where we’ve really focused—our energy is making sure that we go through the more difficult work of managing the long-term health of our patients.”

#5556. A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

Researchers have identified a protein that may play an important role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising new target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

The protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance

Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

To investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising New Direction for Diabetes Treatment

Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

The study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment."

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?

Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan plans to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore new strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he said. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution."

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

#5555. Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

Some of Europe's most famous medieval manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have revealed an extraordinary secret hidden in their pages. Scientists have discovered ancient viral DNA preserved in the animal skins used to make parchment, opening a new window into the 3,500-year history of sheeppox virus (SPPV).

The discovery was made by an international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD). By analyzing parchment from centuries-old documents, the researchers uncovered the first genetic evidence that this destructive disease was spreading through European sheep flocks long before modern times.

Sheeppox is highly contagious and can spread through a flock with alarming speed. It can kill large numbers of infected animals, particularly young sheep, while also causing major economic losses by reducing wool, meat, and milk production.

Ancient Manuscripts Preserve the DNA of Deadly Viruses

Published in Science Advances, the new study reconstructs more than 3,500 years of sheeppox virus evolution. Researchers identified viral DNA in several historically important medieval manuscripts, revealing that documents preserved for their cultural significance can also contain valuable biological evidence.

Among the manuscripts examined was the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, considered one of the finest surviving illuminated manuscripts from the early Anglo-Saxon period. The researchers also studied older works, including the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries, along with other medieval manuscripts from Britain and continental Europe.

The secret lies in the parchment itself. Before paper became widely available, manuscripts were often produced using carefully prepared animal hides, including skins from sheep, goats, and cattle. These materials can preserve traces of an animal's biological history, including evidence of infections present when it died.

In several manuscripts, the researchers detected sheeppox virus DNA on multiple pages. These findings indicate that infected animals had supplied some of the skins used to produce the documents.

An especially surprising discovery involved viral DNA found on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Because sheeppox primarily infects sheep, the results raise two possibilities: the virus may occasionally have infected other livestock species, or viral material may have contaminated the skins during parchment production.

Historic Books Become Unexpected Disease Archives

"The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA. It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past," said Louis L'Hôte, PhD candidate at UCD and lead author of the study.

"These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies -- such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia."

The findings suggest that libraries and archives may hold far more information about historical diseases than previously recognized. Manuscripts that have survived for hundreds of years could provide genetic evidence of livestock outbreaks that left few other records.

"Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft, but we are beginning to understand just how much of the past it has retained. This project shows that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period," said Dr. Kevin G. Daly, Associate Professor at UCD School of Agriculture and Food Science and the study's supervising author.

"This kind of exciting, surprising discovery is only possible when researchers from a range of disciplines come together to share their expertise and data -- a generosity and trust that collaborative science depends on."

The project brought together specialists in genetics, history, virology, protein chemistry, and conservation, allowing the team to investigate the manuscripts from both historical and biological perspectives.

Ancient Sheep Teeth Reveal 3,700 Years of Disease

The medieval manuscripts were only part of the investigation. To trace the disease further into the past, the scientists also examined DNA recovered from sheep teeth dating to the Bronze Age.

Teeth are particularly useful for studying ancient infections because they can protect genetic material for thousands of years, often preserving evidence that has disappeared from other skeletal remains.

The researchers identified the oldest known genetic traces of sheeppox virus in sheep teeth recovered from ancient pastoralist settlements in the Eurasian steppe. When combined with the manuscript findings, this evidence shows that the disease has affected livestock for more than 3,700 years.

To investigate how the virus developed, the team compared ancient viral DNA with genetic sequences from modern viruses. Their analysis suggests that the main branches of the capripoxvirus family (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus) separated from one another sometime between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago.

That estimated timeline coincides with major changes in human history, including the domestication of livestock and the large-scale movement of sheep from the Eurasian steppe into Europe. These movements may have played an important role in the virus's long history of transmission.

A Deadly Virus That Has Barely Changed in Thousands of Years

One of the study's most striking findings was how little the sheeppox virus has changed genetically over the past several thousand years. Unlike some other viruses, its genome appears to have remained remarkably stable despite its long history of infecting livestock.

Understanding that stability could help scientists identify the genetic changes that originally allowed the virus to become an effective sheep pathogen.

The discovery also has immediate relevance. Sheeppox remains a serious threat to livestock farming, with outbreaks continuing to cause substantial economic damage.

"People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen -- there is currently an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage," said Louis L'Hôte.

"Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia."

L'Hôte added: "This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future."

By uncovering viral DNA in both medieval manuscripts and prehistoric animal remains, the researchers have demonstrated a powerful new way to investigate the history of infectious diseases. Their work suggests that materials preserved for entirely different purposes may contain valuable clues about the emergence, spread, and evolution of pathogens that continue to affect the world today.

The research was funded by Taighde Éireann-Research Ireland and the European Research Council. Led by UCD, the project involved more than 30 institutions in Ireland and internationally, including Trinity College Dublin, the Helmholtz Institute for One Health, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, the University of Leicester, Cambridge University, and the University of Copenhagen.

#5552. Rents Rise Annually for First Time in 3 Years as Multifamily Building Boom Stalls

The median asking rent posted its first annual increase in more than three years in October, fueled by a sharp nationwide pullback in multifamily construction.

October marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly rental report. The increase was modest, with the median asking rent rising by just $1 to $1,692, but the underlying data suggests more hikes could follow.

Larger units drove the rebound. Two-bedrooms led the way, with median asking rent rising 0.3% year over year to $1,889, followed by one-bedrooms, which edged up 0.1% to $1,566.

Meanwhile, studio rents continued to lag, falling 1.2% from October 2025 to $1,411.

"I see this as the market beginning to rebalance," Lissette Calderon, CEO of Neology Group, a Miami-based real estate development firm, tells Realtor.com. "We had an extraordinary amount of new supply delivered over the last few years, and it takes time for that inventory to be absorbed. With construction slowing and demand for rental housing remaining strong, I expect rent growth to gradually return, particularly in markets where employment and household growth continue to support housing demand."

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu confirms that last month's rent turnaround hinges on a shifting supply pipeline.

The post-pandemic multifamily construction boom of 2021–22 flooded the market with fresh rental units completed in 2023–25, keeping prices in check.

Now, a broad cooling in multifamily construction is easing downward pressure on rent, just as high mortgage rates continue to keep families in the rental market.

"The path ahead largely depends on whether new multifamily deliveries remain strong enough to outpace that demand," says Xu.

Multifamily developers remain pessimistic about current building conditions, according to the latest quarterly survey from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) released last week.

The NAHB's Multifamily Production Index (MPI) had a reading of 41 out of 100, down 5 points year over year. Any reading below 50 indicates that more builders view market conditions negatively than positively.

"It is not surprising that the MPI is down year over year given supply-side headwinds such as high interest rates and a rising rental vacancy rate," says NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau's Housing Vacancy Survey, the national rental vacancy rate reached 7.6% in the third quarter, the highest level since early 2014.

Kip Lewis, chairman of NAHB’s Multifamily Council, also points to construction costs rising relative to rents, along with delays getting projects approved and connected to roads and utilities.

"As a result, many projects are taking longer to complete," says Lewis.

Echoing Lewis, Calderon says the building pace comes down to the economics of development.

"Construction costs, financing terms, insurance, and operating expenses all affect whether a project can move forward," she says. "When projected rents don’t support the total cost, securing debt and equity becomes more challenging. Developers want to build, but the numbers have to work."

A closer look at the housing data reveals just how dramatically multifamily construction has shifted over the past three years.

Between 2023 and 2025, roughly 1.5 million units in buildings with five or more units were completed, an average of 499,000 per year, up 37.7% from 2020–22.

Those newly completed units boosted the total rental stock by 3.2%, driven by the multifamily starts boom of 2021–23, when ground was broken on more than 1.45 million units.

That surge in rental construction is now fading. In the third quarter of 2026, the multifamily pipeline shrank significantly across the board, with starts averaging 403,000, down more than 9% from a year ago amid soaring financing and construction costs. Units under construction similarly pulled back, averaging 674,000, marking a year-over-year decline of 2.7%.

Completions took the biggest hit, plunging 26% from a year ago to an annualized rate of 330,000 new rental units in the third quarter as the 2023–24 cooldown in housing starts worked its way through the pipeline.

"Given the year-over-year decline in units under construction and higher construction costs, we do not expect deliveries to rebound over the next 12 months," says Xu.

That outlook aligns with NAHB’s 2027 forecast, which predicts a further decline in multifamily starts.

"A thinner pipeline could create pressure in markets where demand continues to grow, but it doesn’t necessarily mean we’re headed for a severe shortage or another sharp increase in rents," says Calderon. "That will depend on how much existing inventory remains available, local employment and household growth, and what is already under construction."

At the regional level, multifamily completions fell year over year everywhere in the third quarter due to fewer starts in 2023–24. The Northeast saw the most dramatic pullback, with finished units dropping nearly 50% from 2025 levels.

"Thinner deliveries could further push up rents in Northeast metros, especially those that have already returned to year-over-year growth, such as Philadelphia and Pittsburgh," says Xu.

The South came in a distant second, with completions falling 28% year over year, followed by the Midwest (-17.9%) and the West (-14.2%).

At the same time, units under construction fell over 11% in the Northeast and 8.8% in the South from a year ago, but increased 4.5% in the West and 12.9% in the Midwest, pointing to a split in active pipelines.

Despite the Midwest's robust building activity, rents are on the rise in several major market metros, including Chicago (+3.2%), St. Louis (+3.2%), and Minneapolis (+2.0%).

When it comes to new groundbreakings, starts in the Northeast surged a staggering 48.4% year over year, making it the only region in positive territory.

“Because projects take about two years to complete in the Northeast, that rebound is unlikely to lift deliveries in 2027," warns Xu.

By contrast, starts fell 12.4% in the West, 16.5% in the South, and 29.2% in the Midwest.

"I remain optimistic about South Florida over the long term, while recognizing that each project needs to be evaluated on its own merits," says Calderon. "For us, that means looking closely at location, the renter we’re serving, competing supply, and the total cost of delivery."

For renters in Western markets such as Los Angeles and Denver, who have seen some relief in asking rents, the slowdown in new construction could reverse that trajectory going forward.

A separate study from RentCafe broadly dovetails with the Realtor.com findings, reinforcing the narrative that the supply of rental units is shrinking nationwide.

Based on data from Yardi Matrix, a commercial real estate intelligence platform that relies on a distinct methodology from Realtor.com, the report found that new apartment construction dropped 27% in 2026, with the Northeast standing out as the sole region to see building activity rise, led by New York City.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5551. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

#5548. Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected new weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.

The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.

The research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.

Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.

According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.

One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.

The researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies."

Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.

A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results

The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.

To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.

The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.

The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments.

With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.

Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive

One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.

The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.

Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.

In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.

Importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.

Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?

The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.

"Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.

Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.

For now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.

If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.

Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

Other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.

#5546. HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers expand into booming peptide market

HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers expand into booming peptide market" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Direct-to-consumer health companies Noom and Hims & Hers are making a play for the booming peptide market as the federal government loosens restrictions on compounded treatments.

The companies are betting that peptides could be the next big thing in consumer health. For Noom, the new peptide offering extends the company's business beyond weight loss into the broader longevity and wellness market. Hims & Hers signaled months ago that it was ready to tap into the multi-billion-dollar peptide market.

Federal policy shifts and U.S. Food and Drug Administration enforcement discretion around compounded peptides have opened new pathways for telehealth and compounding pharmacies.

On Tuesday, Noom launched OpenRx as a separate peptide and preventive health brand. At launch, OpenRx offers two injectable options: sermorelin, a peptide frequently prescribed for muscle support, and NAD+, a coenzyme frequently prescribed for energy. OpenRx also offers two oral dissolvable tablet options: the first formulation combines the peptides PT-141 and oxytocin with tadalafil to support sexual health. The second ODT formulation is the peptide oxytocin to support intimacy.

Noom says it plans to expand into other areas including recovery, muscle health, skin, gut health and sleep. Peptides are small pieces of protein that occur naturally in the body and help control functions such as growth, healing and appetite.

“Peptides are an important portion of the formulary of healthy aging,” Geoff Cook, CEO of Noom, said in a statement. “OpenRx enables our flagship Noom brand to deepen into cardiometabolic health while the new brand OpenRx supports patients with conditions too often neglected by traditional care models, like energy, muscle composition, skin health, sexual health, sleep, and recovery. Together, both brands support the same mission: to empower everyone, everywhere to live better longer – every day.”

Noom says every OpenRx prescription is written by a licensed clinician following an evaluation of the patient’s health history, goals and clinical appropriateness. Treatments are fulfilled through Noom’s U.S.-based pharmacy network, which operates under state boards of pharmacy oversight and adheres to USP compounding standards, the company said.

Noom is currently reviewing BPC-157 and TB-500 as part of its ongoing process of evaluating emerging treatments for inclusion in our formulary, Jeffrey Egler, M.D., Noom's chief medical officer, said in a statement. "Each therapy offered by OpenRx is selected because our clinical team and I believe it is appropriate for improving patient health. The process involves continuous monitoring of safety-related signals, gathering the judgment of our medical directors and the medical directors of affiliated clinical networks based on years of prescribing experience with the compounds in question, ensuring a compliant and stable supply chain, sourcing of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and setting up processes for compliance with state and federal adverse event reporting guidelines," Egler said.

Online health and wellness brand Hims & Hers announced earlier this month it planned to roll out a peptides business. As part of the company's new Peptides+ specialty, launched today, it plans to initially sell five U.S.-compounded peptide and longevity treatments—Sermorelin, NAD+, Glutathione, Vitamin B12 and L-Carnitine, with plans to add more peptides and therapies over time.

The company also plans to offer U.S.-made BPC-157 and TB-500 "consistent with regulatory requirements," the company said.

A survey the company conducted in October of 2,000 adults found that more than half (55%) said they were interested in or curious about peptide therapies, and 40% of U.S. adults say they are interested or very interested in a telehealth offering of injectable prescription treatments, including peptides and other compounded treatments. Nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults (9%) say they currently use peptides, not including FDA-approved peptides such as Ozempic, Wegovy and insulin, the survey found.

Peptides are in the spotlight due to the massive success of FDA-approved GLP-1 weight loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which are peptide drugs. Wellness influencers and biohackers on social media are promoting other lab-made peptides for fast-tracked healing, anti-aging and muscle growth.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed looser federal rules on trendy, unapproved peptide injections. In July, an FDA advisory committee recommended broader access to six unapproved peptides. The panel recommended adding these six substances to the Section 503A Bulks List, which would remove the restrictions on how they are produced by compounders, Fierce Pharma reported.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Kennedy has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued in late October, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

But medical experts have raised safety and clinical evidence questions around unapproved or experimental compounds. The American Medical Association (AMA) publicly opposes the Trump administration’s plan to make certain unapproved peptides more widely available for human use.

In a letter (PDF) to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the AMA pushed back what it called a "rushed" decision to permit the compounding of certain peptides because they have not been approved for safe use by the FDA.

Unproven peptides may pose serious health risks, including allergic reactions, infections, hormonal imbalances and other unexpected side effects, according to the FDA website.

"We should not bypass the science and put patients at risk by making them guinea pigs for unapproved drugs," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement. "If these substances are safe and effective, the evidence should demonstrate that through the FDA’s rigorous review process."

Hims & Hers' peptide therapy program provides a "clinically guided, personalized plan" for consumers "backed by a licensed provider who understands these therapies," according to Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., chief medical officer of the Hims brand.

Hims & Hers wants to "set the standard" for peptide therapy and offer consistency in the quality of the products, Vinjamoori said in an interview on the sidelines of the HLTH conference this week.

"If you think about what we have to bring to the table with our scale and resources, I would argue there's no one better equipped to do it than us," Vinjamoori said.

Hims & Hers has invested in its supply chain and expanded its domestic manufacturing facilities. In 2025, the company acquired a Menlo Park peptide facility to run API validation and stability testing to support its specialized peptide offerings.

"That's why we're investing in our supply chain and doing a lot of the hard work that, frankly, is not the fastest path to making these available. There are pharmacies that are already out there that are making these available, and there are companies out there that will simply just plug into those pharmacies and service patients. But there are inconsistencies," he noted.

Until now, getting these types of medications has often meant relying on unreliable and unregulated online sellers, or a high-cost longevity clinic, Hims & Hers executives said. Hims & Hers' peptides offering gives consumers more accessible care, "backed by real medical leadership and with consistent clinical oversight," the company said in a press release.

Hims & Hers believes its scale gives it an opportunity and responsibility to help build the evidence base around peptides, using growing patient interest not just to expand access but to better understand how the treatments can be used safely and effectively, Vinjamoori said.

Expanding into peptides fits with Hims & Hers' ongoing focus on personalized health, he noted. "We started with sexual health, moved on to hair loss, and then we've continued to broaden into other categories such as hormone replacement, GLP-1s, and now peptides, and many others to come. And the common theme in all of this is that we're talking about helping people accomplish a specific goal that they have. We're not talking about curing a disease or treating a disease per se," he said. "We're talking about, 'Hey, there's something you want to do in your life that you're not able to do right now. Let's help you figure out how we can put together a plan to help you accomplish that."

"This is a big part of the future of medicine itself," Vinjamoori added. "It's been the missing part of the equation, where we've been very focused on treating and responding to disease, but not as much, not just on prevention, but really on helping people use their health as an asset and as a tool to help them accomplish what they want in life."

With Hims & Hers' peptide therapy offering, consumers start with a clinical visit with a licensed provider that includes a comprehensive intake of health history and goals. The company said a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies assesses each individual and, if appropriate, tailors a personalized protocol to their needs.

Hims & Hers treatments are compounded in the U.S. and dispensed directly by licensed, U.S. pharmacies regulated by state boards of pharmacy and "held to rigorous quality and safety standards," the company said.

The buzz around peptides ties into consumers' growing interest in taking control of their health "driven by the cultural zeitgeist moment," Vinjamoori told Fierce Healthcare.

"There's a variety of different factors that catalyze that. I think the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a lot of it for a variety of reasons. I think you see accelerations in biotechnology where people now see something like GLP-1s that can help with a problem that seemed intractable before. I think people are now interested in figuring out what is the range of solutions that could help me. I also think peptides represent something that has a lot of promise, a lot of excitement," he said.

"But there are also some cautions that we need to take as well. Something we think a lot about is how do we meet this moment of excitement and enthusiasm with some degree of rigor and guardrails," Vinjamoori said.

"It starts with the product itself. How do we ensure the quality? The compounds are of the highest quality and are compounded in the most rigorous way, made available in the most rigorous way. That's why we are trying to have as much oversight as we can into the full process of making these available," he said.

He asserted that informed consent and transparency with consumers are critical. "I've spent a lot of time with the team to make sure that we understand that people have this enthusiasm, but we need to make sure that they understand what they're getting into. There is a difference between this and FDA-approved therapies," he said.

"Sometimes people should try the standard of care before they engage with some of these things, and so we want to make sure we have these conversations with people openly and honestly. But at the same time, we also want to respect their choice," he added.

Hims & Hers Peptides+ is available with its Care+ program that gives customers access to twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress, unlimited support and ongoing check-ins from a dedicated care team. Customers can also message providers trained in peptide therapy 24/7 with any questions. The Hims Men’s panel includes at-home blood collection and access to lab tests that provide insights across 22 biomarkers, including testosterone, vitamin D, and cholesterol. The Hers Women’s panel tests 22 biomarkers across hormones, vitamins, and heart health.

#5545. Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. In a study involving more than 120,000 older adults, researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed) found that patients taking certain medications to strengthen their bones were significantly less likely to develop dementia.

The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures. The findings suggest that these established treatments could potentially serve a second purpose by helping protect the aging brain. The research, conducted by scientists in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed's LKS Faculty of Medicine, was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia.

More than 55 million people worldwide currently live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050. The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a major global health priority. Although the first medications designed to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have recently gained approval, their high costs, limited suitability for some patients, and questions about their effectiveness remain important challenges.

These obstacles have increased interest in finding affordable ways to prevent or delay dementia before symptoms develop. One promising approach is to identify existing medications that might offer benefits beyond the conditions they were originally designed to treat.

The Surprising Connection Between Bone Health and Dementia

Osteoporosis and dementia often affect the same older adults. Osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures, while dementia progressively affects memory, thinking, and the ability to carry out everyday activities. The two conditions also share several risk factors, including older age, being female, and low levels of physical activity.

Previous research by the same HKUMed team established that osteoporosis and fractures are independent risk factors for dementia. The researchers also found that people already living with dementia face an increased likelihood of falling and breaking bones.

This relationship raises an intriguing possibility: medications that treat osteoporosis might also help reduce dementia risk.

Among the most commonly prescribed osteoporosis treatments are alendronate and zoledronate, both of which belong to the NBP drug class. These medications work by slowing the breakdown of bone tissue, helping maintain bone strength and reduce the likelihood of fractures.

Scientists have also begun uncovering evidence that some of the biological processes influenced by these drugs may be involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. This overlap has prompted researchers to investigate whether NBPs might provide benefits for the brain as well as the skeleton.

Study of 120,000 Patients Finds Up to 24% Lower Dementia Risk

To explore this possibility, the HKUMed researchers examined electronic medical records from across Hong Kong, analyzing data from more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older. All participants had osteoporosis or fragility fractures, which are breaks that can occur after relatively minor injuries because the bones have become weakened.

The records covered the period from 2005 through 2020, allowing the team to investigate how different osteoporosis treatments were associated with dementia risk over time.

The results revealed a notable difference. Patients taking NBPs had a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared with patients who received no osteoporosis medication.

The association was even stronger when NBP users were compared with patients taking other types of osteoporosis drugs. In that comparison, dementia risk was 24% lower among those receiving NBPs.

Women and patients who had experienced hip fractures appeared to show particularly strong associations between NBP treatment and reduced dementia risk.

The researchers also estimated that treating 48 patients with NBPs over five years could potentially prevent one case of dementia. If future research confirms that the medications directly reduce dementia risk, the implications could be substantial, particularly for older adults who already need treatment for osteoporosis.

Because the findings come from an observational study, they do not establish that the drugs themselves prevent dementia. However, they provide evidence supporting further investigation into whether these medications could help delay or prevent cognitive decline.

Could Existing Osteoporosis Drugs Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Professor Cheung Ching-lung, Associate Professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed, believes the findings highlight the possibility that a familiar osteoporosis treatment could deliver two important health benefits.

"Our study provides evidence that NBPs may offer dual benefits in strengthening bones and reducing fracture risk, as well as potentially preventing ADRD. Their potential neuroprotective role provides an empirical basis and supports future research on the actual effectiveness of this medication in preventing or delaying cognitive decline associated with ADRD."

The potential advantage of this approach is that NBPs are already widely available and have an established history of use in treating osteoporosis. Rather than developing an entirely new medication from scratch, researchers could investigate whether these existing treatments offer additional protection for people at elevated risk of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant as populations around the world grow older and the number of people affected by dementia continues to rise.

"These findings are significant as they demonstrate a potential approach for reducing dementia risk in a vulnerable population using safe and widely available NBPs. In our rapidly aging society, these findings suggest that while waiting for the novel therapies, existing medications can also provide additional protection for high-risk populations," said Professor Cheung.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether NBPs can directly prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Nevertheless, the results suggest that medications already prescribed to protect aging bones may also have an important role to play in protecting brain health.

The research was led by Professor Cheung Ching-lung of the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed. Dr Sing Chor-wing, from the same department, served as the study's first author.

Additional researchers included Professor Chan Koon-ho, Dr Patrick Chiu Ka-chun, and Professor Kathryn Tan Choon-beng, all from the Department of Medicine in the School of Clinical Medicine at HKUMed.

Materials provided by The University of Hong Kong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5543. Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million

Angela Huffman, a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH, and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH, sheep farm.

On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky.

The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town.

"We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com®. Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant.

"What does that do to the community?" she says.

Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures.

Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone.

Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment blocking large data centers within the limits of the 6,600-person town.

"They wanted to use about a third of the water the whole town uses today," Huffman says. "I'm not against AI or development, but can a town of this size absorb a development like that?"

But the state already hosts dozens of large centers. And they already exact a cost.

A new study shows that the state's data center tax break derived its schools of almost $374 million in revenue in 2025 alone.

Republican Gov. Mike DeWine paused the tax breaks in May after the state realized developers were exempted from $2.1 billion in taxes in 2024 and 2025, far more than initally projected. Gov.-elect Amy Acton has promised further scrutiny.

Good Jobs First and Policy Matters Ohio studied where those missing tax dollars would have gone. The state's Fair School Funding Plan allocates some sales tax to schools. So by exempting data center developers from the 5.75% sales tax, those schools missed out on revenue.

“Ohio lawmakers made a choice to give data center companies a blank check, and now Ohio’s schools are paying the price,” said Hannah Halbert, Policy Matters Ohio’s executive director. “In 2025 alone, the state gave up enough revenue from this single tax break to fully update the Fair School Funding plan and close the gap.”

This comes at a time when homeowners were being asked to make up the difference. Many Ohio schools aimed to raise money through levies this year, but many were unsuccessful. The Ohio Policy Education Institute found just 24 of 66 levies on the May 2026 ballot had passed.

Upper Sandusky's school district was one of the losers—missing out on $383,000 in revenue, according to the report. While voters have approved levies for its schools in 2015, 2018, and 2023, it's still been forced to cancel classes this year because it can't install air conditioning in century-old buildings that are too expensive to rebuild.

"Our schools were struggling," Huffman says. "It tells you a lot about when these big tech companies come along, and if they are paying their fair share."

Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. NBC exit polls show 76% of voters opposed data center building in their communities, and a majority considered them "crucial" to their votes.

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

That's despite a major spending spree by the industry. Ohio was barraged with $1.8 million in data center ads in the fall, Pew Research Center found—more than Texas, Wisconsin, and other large states. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million backing Republican Sen. John Husted, who lost reelection to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3.

Developers, after all, have big plans in the state, having pitched $168.7 billion in new projects.

Regulation of data center developments and AI could be a major factor for new Democratic leaders in Columbus and Washington, DC. Sober to that reality, tech stocks tanked after the election.

Acton says she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers. She wants to see them cover their utility costs, build with union labor, and abide by environmental standards. She also says she wants to see incentives "reined in" for the large developments.

Artificial intelligence companies have spent the days since the election promising they'll work with cities and residents on data centers. OpenAI published a "blueprint for responsible development" promising to slow the technology.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone cited a commitment "to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities."

Ohio isn't alone, either. Virginia, another data center hot spot, spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. It and other hot spots like California and Texas have also moved to restrict data center developments this year.

A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also said that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

Ohio, in the meantime, has seen its housing situation worsen in the past few years. National Housing Conference data put the state first in the union for how quickly middle-income earners have been priced out. The number of jobs that can afford a typical home at a 10% down payment fell about 41% from 2020 to 2025. Teachers, firefighters, and retail supervisors are among those priced out of median-priced homes.

But data center advocates say the large developments are still necessary in the modern economy.

Dan Diorio, vice president for public policy at the Data Center Coalition, told the Ohio Tax Credit Authority that the developments benefit all people and businesses, not just AI companies.

"This is a far more efficient way of doing all the computing, processing, and storage that we need to facilitate our daily lives in the 21st century economy," Diorio said at the May hearing in Columbus. "The need for connectivity, for the internet, is driving the digital infrastructure that supports that."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5542. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."
